newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil vote scandal rumbles on with new report.
newsitem.headline: Brazil vote scandal rumbles on with new report.

text.p: A newspaper that has been reporting a vote-buying scandal alleged on Thursday a government minister gave a television concession as well as cash to a lawmaker in return for his vote on a key bill.

Daily Folha de Sao Paulo, which rocked the Brazilian capital and financial markets this week with its reports of an alleged cash-for-votes scam, claimed it had tapes of a telephone conversation in which the lawmaker refers to the deal.

In the purported conversation, Ronivon Santiago told an unidentified "Mr. X" he and Communications Minister Sergio Motta fixed a bidding process for the television concession in the remote Amazonian state of Acre.

A spokesman for Motta, who is a close friend of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, said the minister would not respond to the new report. "These allegations are very weak. It looks like the Folha de Sao Paulo is running out of steam," he said.
Stock markets were unimpressed, too. Share prices, which fell 3.42 percent amid panic on Wednesday, recovered on Thursday and were up 2.58 percent at midday on the Sao Paulo stock exchange.
"The market read the newspapers today and breathed a sigh of relief. It thinks the crisis has leveled off," said Miriam Leitao, a financial commentator with national Globo television.

Motta on Wednesday vigorously denied any role in the scandal and said there was "not one solid accusation or fact" in the allegations he helped buy votes for a bill which would allow Cardoso to run for re-election next year.

The bill was approved in the Chamber of Deputies in January in what was considered the biggest political victory of the Cardoso administration. It was due to be put to a first of two votes in the Senate next week and would allow presidents, state governors and mayors to run for a second consecutive term.
An internal congressional panel summoned five deputies, two state governors and Motta to defend themselves against the allegations and was due to announce its findings next week.

Left-wing political parties said the investigation lacked teeth and said they want to set up a wide-ranging parliamentary inquiry, known as a CPI. "Whoever's against the CPI, has something to hide," said Workers Party (PT) deputy Jose Genoino.
The PT already has enough signatures for a CPI in the Chamber of Deputies but needs votes from government-allied parties in order to set up the inquiry immediately.
Government whips said a CPI would ruin their efforts to approve civil service and pension reforms delayed for nearly two years because of stiff opposition.
